Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional unital algebra over a field $k$. Write
$S_1,\ldots,S_t$ for representatives of the isomorphism classes of simple
left $A$-modules, and choose a finite-dimensional projective cover
$q_i\colon P_i\twoheadrightarrow S_i$ for each $i$. Then the split
Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional projective left $A$-modules
([[def-split-grothendieck-group-of-an-additive-category]]) is the free abelian
group with basis $[P_1],\ldots,[P_t]$. In particular, each selected cover is
indecomposable, the $P_i$ are pairwise nonisomorphic, and every finite
dimensional projective is a finite direct sum of them. This result makes no
claim that the Cartan map to the short-exact-sequence group $G_0(A)$ is
invertible.

Let $\mathcal C$ be an essentially small abelian category in which every object
has finite length. Let $\operatorname{Simp}(\mathcal C)$ be the set of
isomorphism classes of simple objects. The homomorphism

$$\Phi:\mathbb Z[\operatorname{Simp}(\mathcal C)]\longrightarrow G_0(\mathcal C),\qquad e_{[S]}\longmapsto[S],$$

is an isomorphism. For any object $M$ and simple object $S$, the coordinate of
$[M]$ under $\Phi^{-1}$ at $e_{[S]}$ is $[M:S]$, the number of composition
factors isomorphic to $S$ in a composition series of $M$.

Let $k$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital associative
$\mathbb Z$-graded $k$-algebra. A **graded-simple module** here means a
nonzero finite-dimensional graded left $A$-module whose only graded submodules
are $0$ and itself. Internal shift acts on graded-simple isomorphism classes
by $[S]\mapsto[S\{r\}]$ for $r\in\mathbb Z$. There are finitely many shift
orbits of graded-simple isomorphism classes. For each orbit choose a
representative $S_i$ and a finite graded projective cover
$p_i:P_i\twoheadrightarrow S_i$, whose kernel is superfluous among graded
submodules. Then

$$
\{[S_i]\}_i\text{ is a }\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]\text{-basis of }G_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(A), \qquad \{[P_i]\}_i\text{ is a }\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]\text{-basis of }K_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(A).
$$

In particular, both modules have the same finite rank, the number of graded
simple shift orbits. If $A=0$, both bases are empty and both groups are zero.
No positivity assumption on the grading of $A$ is made.

Let $k$ be a field and let $A=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z}A_i$ be a finite-dimensional, unital, associative, $\mathbb Z$-graded $k$-algebra. Let $\mathcal M^{\mathrm{gr}}_{\mathrm{fd}}(A)$ be the category of finite-dimensional graded left $A$-modules and degree-zero maps, and let $\mathcal P^{\mathrm{gr}}_{\mathrm{fd}}(A)$ be its full subcategory of finite graded projective modules. Define

$$G_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(A):=G_0\!\left(\mathcal M^{\mathrm{gr}}_{\mathrm{fd}}(A)\right),\qquad K_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(A):=K_0^{\mathrm{split}}\!\left(\mathcal P^{\mathrm{gr}}_{\mathrm{fd}}(A)\right).$$

Here $G_0$ uses all short-exact-sequence relations, while $K_0^{\mathrm{split}}$ uses only direct-sum relations. Let $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{fd}}(A)$ be the category of finite-dimensional ungraded left $A$-modules and put $G_0(A):=G_0(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{fd}}(A))$. The notation $K_0(A)$ is the split Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional projective left $A$-modules from [[def-split-grothendieck-group-of-an-additive-category]].

For $r\in\mathbb Z$, internal shift is $(M\{r\})_d:=M_{d-r}$. It acts on generators by

$$v^r[M]:=[M\{r\}],\qquad v^r[P]:=[P\{r\}],$$

for $[M]\in G_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(A)$ and $[P]\in K_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(A)$. These actions make both groups modules over $\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$, with $v[M]=[M\{1\}]$ and $v[P]=[P\{1\}]$.

The graded Cartan homomorphism is

$$c_A^{\mathrm{gr}}:K_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(A)\longrightarrow G_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(A),\qquad [P]\longmapsto[P].$$

It is $\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$-linear. The ungraded Cartan homomorphism is

$$c_A:K_0(A)\longrightarrow G_0(A),\qquad [P]\longmapsto[P].$$

Neither map is asserted to be injective or surjective.

For every ring $R$, the category $R\text{-}\mathbf{Mod}$ of left $R$-modules is
an abelian category.

An **abelian category** is an additive category ([[def-additive-category]]) in
which every morphism has a kernel and a cokernel, and in which for every
morphism $f$ the canonical comparison morphism

$$\operatorname{coim}(f)\longrightarrow\operatorname{im}(f)$$

constructed in
[[thm-the-canonical-morphism-from-the-coimage-to-the-image-exists-and-is-unique]]
is an isomorphism.

The first two clauses are Grothendieck's AB1, while the invertibility of the
canonical map is this page's working form of AB2.

An **additive category** is a preadditive category
([[def-preadditive-category]]) with all finite biproducts.

Equivalently, a preadditive category is additive when it has a zero object and
binary biproducts: a zero object is both initial and terminal
([[def-initial-terminal-and-zero-object]]) and therefore supplies both the empty
coproduct and the empty product
([[prop-empty-limits-and-colimits-are-terminal-and-initial-objects]]); their
canonical comparison is the unique endomorphism of the zero object and hence
the identity, so this is an empty biproduct. Meanwhile,
binary biproducts iterate
using the canonical associativity and unitality isomorphisms
([[prop-biproducts-are-associative-commutative-and-unital-up-to-canonical-isomorphism]])
to give every finite biproduct.

An object $A$ of an abelian category has **finite length** when it admits a
composition series in the sense of
[[def-composition-series-and-composition-factors-of-an-object]].

Its **length** $\ell(A)$ is the number of successive simple factors in any
composition series. The Jordan-Hölder theorem
[[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-in-an-abelian-category]] makes this number
independent of the chosen series.

A **composition series** of an object $A$ in an abelian category is a finite
strict chain of subobjects

$$0=A_0\;<\;A_1\;<\;\cdots\;<\;A_n=A$$

such that every quotient object $A_i/A_{i-1}$ is simple
([[def-simple-object]], [[def-the-quotient-of-an-object-by-a-subobject]]).

The simple quotient objects $A_i/A_{i-1}$ are the **composition factors** of
the series.

An **essential epimorphism** of modules is a surjective homomorphism
$\pi:P\to M$ whose kernel is superfluous: whenever $N\le P$ and
$N+\ker\pi=P$, one already has $N=P$.

A **projective cover** of $M$ is an essential epimorphism $\pi:P\to M$ with
$P$ projective in the sense of [[def-projective-module]] and
[[thm-projective-module-characterizations]].

The superfluous-kernel language is the one used on this page, motivated by
[[lem-radical-of-a-finite-length-module-is-superfluous]].

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Z$-graded $k$-algebra over a field,
and let $X$ be a finite-dimensional graded left $A$-module. There is a
degree-zero epimorphism $p\colon P\twoheadrightarrow X$ in
$\operatorname{GrMod}_0(A)$ ([[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]])
with $P$ finite graded projective and
$K:=\ker p$ satisfying

$$ N+K=P\quad\Longrightarrow\quad N=P $$

for every graded submodule $N\le P$. We call such a map a **finite graded
projective cover**; superfluity of its kernel is tested among graded
submodules, as appropriate in $\operatorname{GrMod}_0(A)$
([[def-essential-epimorphism-and-projective-cover]]). Any two finite graded
projective covers of $X$ are isomorphic over $X$: if $q\colon Q\twoheadrightarrow
X$ is another, there is a degree-zero isomorphism $\phi\colon P\to Q$ with
$q\phi=p$ ([[def-finitely-generated-graded-projective-module]]). No positivity
assumption on the grading of $A$ is made.
A nonzero homomorphism between simple modules is an isomorphism. Consequently the endomorphism ring of a simple module is a division ring. See [[def-simple-module]].

A left $R$-module $M$ is **simple** if $M\ne0$ and its only submodules are
$0$ and $M$. Equivalently, $M$ has no proper nonzero submodule.

**Ground ring and graded algebras.** Fix a commutative ring $k$. A **graded
$k$-algebra** is a $k$-algebra $A$ in the sense of
[[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]], together with a direct sum
decomposition of $k$-modules

$$A=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z}A_i$$

such that $A_iA_j\subseteq A_{i+j}$ for all $i,j\in\mathbb Z$ and
$1_A\in A_0$. It is **unital and associative** when its underlying ring is;
every graded algebra on this page is unital and associative. Since
$\eta_A(r)=r\,1_A$ and $A_0$ is a $k$-submodule containing $1_A$, the structure
map has image in $A_0$, so each $A_i$ is a $k$-submodule and the scalars act
centrally on $A$.

**Graded modules and bimodules.** A **graded left $A$-module** is a left
$A$-module $M$ with a decomposition $M=\bigoplus_{d\in\mathbb Z}M_d$ of
$k$-modules such that

$$A_iM_d\subseteq M_{i+d}\qquad\text{for all }i,d\in\mathbb Z .$$

A **graded right $A$-module** is a right $A$-module with a decomposition
$M=\bigoplus_dM_d$ such that $M_dA_i\subseteq M_{d+i}$ for all $i,d$. A
**graded $(B,A)$-bimodule** is a $(B,A)$-bimodule ([[def-bimodule]]) that is
graded as a $k$-module and homogeneous under both actions, the two actions
continuing to commute. Both induced $k$-actions must agree with the given
$k$-module structure: $\eta_B(t)m=tm=m\eta_A(t)$ for $t\in k$ and $m\in M$. Elements of $M_d$ are **homogeneous of degree $d$**, and
the decomposition expresses every $m\in M$ uniquely as a finite sum of nonzero
homogeneous components.

**Degree-zero maps.** A map $f:M\to N$ of graded left $A$-modules is
**degree-zero**, or a **graded map**, when it is $A$-linear and
$f(M_d)\subseteq N_d$ for every $d$. The category $\operatorname{GrMod}_0(A)$
has the graded left $A$-modules as objects and the degree-zero maps as
morphisms, with composition of maps. Every $M$ is an object of
$\operatorname{GrMod}_0(A)$ by its own grading, and $A$ is a graded
$(A,A)$-bimodule under left and right multiplication.

**Graded submodules.** A **graded submodule** of a graded left $A$-module $M$ is
a submodule $S\le M$ with $S=\bigoplus_{d\in\mathbb Z}(S\cap M_d)$. Such an $S$
is itself a graded left $A$-module with homogeneous pieces
$S_d:=S\cap M_d$, because $A_iS_d\subseteq A_iM_d\cap S\subseteq M_{i+d}\cap S=S_{i+d}$;
equivalently, $S$ is generated by its homogeneous elements. In particular a
graded submodule is determined by its homogeneous pieces: if
$S=\bigoplus_dS_d$ and $T=\bigoplus_dT_d$ are graded submodules with $S_d=T_d$
for every $d$, then $S=T$.

**Internal shift.** For $r\in\mathbb Z$ and a graded module $M$, the
**internal shift** $M\{r\}$ is the module with

$$(M\{r\})_d:=M_{d-r}\qquad(d\in\mathbb Z),$$

carrying the same scalar action as $M$. Its components are additive subgroups
of $M$ whose sum is direct, so $M\{r\}$ is a $k$-module; and $M\{r\}$ is
graded because

$$A_i(M\{r\})_d=A_iM_{d-r}\subseteq M_{i+d-r}=(M\{r\})_{i+d}$$

for all $i,d$. For a graded bimodule both actions are unchanged, remain
homogeneous and still commute, so $M\{r\}$ is again a graded bimodule. The
shift is invertible: $(M\{r\})\{-r\}=M$, and $M\{0\}=M$. For a graded algebra
$A$, the shifts $A\{r\}$ of the regular bimodule are the modules denoted
$A\{r\}$ elsewhere on this page.

**Dictionary with the published twist.** In the published nonnegative
commutative convention ([[def-graded-ring-and-graded-module]]) the twist $M(a)$
is the graded module with $M(a)_d=M_{d+a}$ for every integer $a$. Substituting
$a=-r$ gives

$$(M\{r\})_d=M_{d-r}=M(-r)_d ,$$

so $M\{r\}=M(-r)$ as graded modules: the internal shift **reverses** the sign of
the published twist parameter. For $r=0$ both conventions agree with $M$.

**No super signs.** The internal degree is a genuine $\mathbb Z$-grading, not a
$\mathbb Z/2$-parity. No sign is inserted into the multiplication, the scalar
action or a degree-zero map merely because elements have nonzero degree; the
balancing relation of the tensor product below is likewise signed by nothing.
These are the unsigned associative conventions for this page; no differential
or signed symmetry on tensor products is part of this definition. They do not
exclude Koszul sign conventions in other categories of graded objects.

**Total internal degree on the balanced tensor product.** Let $A$ be a graded
$k$-algebra, $M$ a graded right $A$-module and $N$ a graded left $A$-module
([[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]]). First use the canonical
decomposition of the ordinary tensor product of the underlying abelian groups
$$M\otimes_{\mathbb Z}N\cong\bigoplus_{i,j\in\mathbb Z}M_i\otimes_{\mathbb Z}N_j.$$
Its inverse sends $m\otimes n$ to the finite sum
$\sum_{i,j}m_i\otimes n_j$, where $m=\sum_i m_i$ and $n=\sum_jn_j$ are their
homogeneous decompositions; the two maps are inverse because they agree with
the identity on homogeneous elementary tensors. Give the summand
$M_i\otimes_{\mathbb Z}N_j$ total degree $i+j$, and write
$G_d:=\bigoplus_{i+j=d}M_i\otimes_{\mathbb Z}N_j$.

The balanced tensor product
$M\otimes_AN=(M\otimes_{\mathbb Z}N)/\mathcal R_A$
([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]), where
$\mathcal R_A$ is generated by the balance relations
$(ma)\otimes n-m\otimes(an)$. These relations are generated by the homogeneous
ones: for $m=\sum_i m_i$, $a=\sum_\ell a_\ell$ and $n=\sum_jn_j$, the relation
is the finite sum of
$(m_i a_\ell)\otimes n_j-m_i\otimes(a_\ell n_j)$ over $i,\ell,j$. Each such
homogeneous relation belongs to $G_{i+\ell+j}$, since the two module actions
preserve total degree. Thus $\mathcal R_A=\bigoplus_d(\mathcal R_A\cap G_d)$,
and

$$M\otimes_AN=\bigoplus_{d\in\mathbb Z}(M\otimes_AN)_d,\qquad (M\otimes_AN)_d:=(G_d+\mathcal R_A)/\mathcal R_A,$$

is a graded abelian group. For homogeneous $m\in M_i$ and $n\in N_j$ the
elementary tensor $m\otimes n$ has **total internal degree** $i+j$; every tensor
is a finite sum of homogeneous elementary tensors, and the balancing relations
used in the quotient are homogeneous. This grading is the only grading used
below, and it introduces no sign.

**Outer actions.** If $M$ is a graded $(B,A)$-bimodule and $N$ a graded left
$A$-module, then the action $b(m\otimes n):=(bm)\otimes n$ of
[[thm-bimodule-actions-induced-on-tensor-products]] makes $M\otimes_AN$ a graded
left $B$-module: the action is homogeneous because homogeneous $b\in B_l$ sends
$m\otimes n$ of degree $i+j$ to an element of degree $l+i+j$. Symmetrically, if
$N$ is a graded $(A,C)$-bimodule, the action
$(m\otimes n)c:=m\otimes(nc)$ makes $M\otimes_AN$ a graded right $C$-module, and
the two outer actions commute when both are present.

**Homogeneous Hom.** For graded left $A$-modules $P,Q$, with
$\operatorname{Hom}_A^{\mathrm{ungr}}(P,Q)$ the abelian group of all $A$-linear
maps $P\to Q$, put

$$\operatorname{Hom}_{A,d}(P,Q):=\bigl\{f\in\operatorname{Hom}_A^{\mathrm{ungr}}(P,Q)\mid f(P_i)\subseteq Q_{i+d}\ \text{for all }i\in\mathbb Z\bigr\},\qquad \operatorname{HOM}_A(P,Q):=\bigoplus_{d\in\mathbb Z}\operatorname{Hom}_{A,d}(P,Q).$$

Each $\operatorname{Hom}_{A,d}(P,Q)$ is a subgroup of
$\operatorname{Hom}_A^{\mathrm{ungr}}(P,Q)$, and the sum is direct: if
$f=\sum_df_d=\sum_df'_d$ with $f_d,f'_d\in\operatorname{Hom}_{A,d}$, then for
$p\in P_i$ the element $f(p)$ has homogeneous components
$f_d(p)\in Q_{i+d}$, and comparison of the graded components in $Q$ gives
$f_d(p)=f'_d(p)$ for every $d$ and $p$, so $f_d=f'_d$. Thus
$\operatorname{HOM}_A(P,Q)$ is a graded abelian group whose degree-$d$ part is
$\operatorname{Hom}_{A,d}(P,Q)$, and the degree-zero morphisms are
$\operatorname{Hom}_{A,0}(P,Q)$. By definition $\operatorname{HOM}_A(P,Q)$
consists of the finite sums of homogeneous $A$-linear maps, so
$\operatorname{HOM}_A(P,Q)\subseteq\operatorname{Hom}_A^{\mathrm{ungr}}(P,Q)$
with equality only when every $A$-linear map has bounded spread in degree.

**The associative left action.** If $M$ is a graded $(B,A)$-bimodule and $Y$ a
graded left $B$-module, then $\operatorname{HOM}_B(M,Y)$ carries a left
$A$-module structure

$$(a\cdot f)(m):=f(ma)\qquad(a\in A,\ m\in M),$$

which is homogeneous: for $a\in A_i$ and $f\in\operatorname{Hom}_{B,d}(M,Y)$ one
has $ma\in M_{l+i}$ for $m\in M_l$, hence $(a\cdot f)(m)\in Y_{l+i+d}$ and
$a\cdot f\in\operatorname{Hom}_{B,d+i}(M,Y)$. The action is associative and
unital by the module axioms of $M$, so $\operatorname{HOM}_B(M,Y)$ is a graded
left $A$-module and an object of $\operatorname{GrMod}_0(A)$. The same formula
defines an action on the full ungraded $\operatorname{Hom}$ group, where it is
denoted by the same symbol.

For any unital associative $\mathbb Z$-graded algebra $A$, the category
$\operatorname{GrMod}_0(A)$ of graded left $A$-modules and degree-zero maps is
abelian. Kernels, images, cokernels and finite biproducts are computed in each
homogeneous degree; a sequence is exact precisely when it is exact degreewise.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]). An **$R$-algebra** is a unital ring $A$ together with a unital ring homomorphism

$$\eta_A:R\longrightarrow A$$

([[def-ring-homomorphism]]) whose image is central: $\eta_A(r)a=a\eta_A(r)$ for every $r\in R$ and $a\in A$. The induced scalar action is $ra:=\eta_A(r)a$, making $A$ an $R$-module and multiplication $A\times A\to A$ bilinear.

An **$R$-algebra homomorphism** $f:A\to B$ is a unital ring homomorphism satisfying $f\circ\eta_A=\eta_B$. Such a map is automatically $R$-linear. An $R$-algebra is **commutative** when its underlying ring is commutative.

If $V$ and $W$ are vector spaces over a field $F$, then
$\mathcal L(V,W)$ is a vector space over $F$ under pointwise addition and
scalar multiplication.

For a field $F$ and naturals $m,n$,
$\dim_FM_{m\times n}(F)=mn$. Consequently, for finite-dimensional $F$-vector
spaces $V,W$,

$$\dim_F\mathcal L(V,W)=(\dim_FV)(\dim_FW).$$

Let $k$ be a field and let $A$ be a finite-dimensional unital associative $k$-algebra. For finite-dimensional projective left $A$-modules $P$ and finite-dimensional left $A$-modules $M$, the generator value $h(P,M):=\dim_k\operatorname{Hom}_A(P,M)$ from [[def-projective-simple-hom-pairing-on-grothendieck-groups]] extends uniquely to a $\mathbb Z$-bilinear pairing $\langle-,-\rangle:K_0(A)\times G_0(A)\to\mathbb Z$.

If $A$ is also $\mathbb Z$-graded and $P,M$ are finite-dimensional graded left $A$-modules with $P$ projective in $\operatorname{GrMod}_0(A)$, the generator value $h_{\mathrm{gr}}(P,M):=\sum_{d\in\mathbb Z}v^d\dim_k\operatorname{Hom}_{A,d}(P,M)$ extends uniquely to a $\mathbb Z$-bilinear pairing $\langle-,-\rangle_{\mathrm{gr}}:K_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(A)\times G_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(A)\to R$, where $R:=\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$.

For all $r,s\in\mathbb Z$ and generator classes $[P],[M]$, $\langle v^r[P],v^s[M]\rangle_{\mathrm{gr}}=v^{s-r}\langle[P],[M]\rangle_{\mathrm{gr}}$. Consequently $\langle fx,gy\rangle_{\mathrm{gr}}=\overline f\,g\,\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathrm{gr}}$ for $f,g\in R$, $x\in K_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(A)$ and $y\in G_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(A)$, with $\overline f(v):=f(v^{-1})$. Thus the first variable is conjugate-linear for the involution $v\mapsto v^{-1}$ and the second is linear. No axiom of choice is used.

Fix a graded $k$-algebra $A$ and let $P$ be a graded left $A$-module
([[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]]). The category
$\operatorname{GrMod}_0(A)$ of graded left $A$-modules and degree-zero maps is
abelian ([[lem-graded-module-kernels-cokernels-and-biproducts-are-degreewise]]).

**Graded projective.** $P$ is **graded projective** when it is a projective
object of $\operatorname{GrMod}_0(A)$ ([[def-projective-object]]): for every
degree-zero epimorphism $q:E\twoheadrightarrow M$ and every degree-zero
$f:P\to M$ there exists a degree-zero $\widetilde f:P\to E$ with
$q\widetilde f=f$. Thus projectivity is tested only against degree-zero
epimorphisms and degree-zero maps, and the lift need not be unique.

**Finitely generated.** $P$ is **finitely generated as a graded left
$A$-module**, or generated by finitely many homogeneous elements, when for some
$n\ge0$ there are homogeneous elements $p_1,\dots,p_n\in P$ with

$$P=A p_1+\cdots+A p_n .$$

By [[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]] this is the same
notion as finite generation of the underlying $A$-module: a finite homogeneous
family is a finite family, and conversely, if $P=\langle S\rangle_A$ for a
finite set $S$, then writing each $s=\sum_es_e$ as its finite sum of nonzero
homogeneous components gives, for every $x=\sum_{s\in S}a_s s\in P$,

$$x=\sum_{s\in S}a_s\sum_es_e=\sum_{s,e}a_s s_e,$$

a finite $A$-linear combination of the homogeneous elements $s_e\in P$; so the
finitely many components of the members of $S$ generate $P$. In particular the
notion does not depend on the chosen finite generating set.

**Finite graded projective.** $P$ is **finite graded projective** when it is
graded projective and generated by finitely many homogeneous elements, that is,
